source.title: From Features to Transformers: Redefining Ranking for Scalable Impact
source.authors: Fedor Borisyuk; Lars Hertel; Ganesh Parameswaran; Gaurav Srivastava; Sudarshan Srinivasa Ramanujam; Borja Ocejo; Peng Du; Andrei Akterskii; Neil Daftary; Shao Tang; Da-Qi Sun; Qiang Charles Xiao; Deepesh Nathani; Mohit Kothari; Yun Dai; Guo-Yao Li; Aman Gupta

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in a production recommender-ranking setting rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling experiments for ranking models, including evaluation loss and AUC under changes in compute and model dimensions. Results about feature ablations, retrieval, setwise ranking and A/B tests do not test the listed scaling-law versions and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own scaling sweeps of a transformer recommender-ranking model (LiGR) on LinkedIn Feed data. It reports evaluation loss (normalized entropy) against training FLOPS and against individual scaled dimensions. That is a new setting with a result on whether loss scaling carries over beyond text pretraining (V5). It fits no power law and reports no exponents.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim to validate scaling laws for ranking: better performance with larger models, more data and longer sequences, and LiGR outperforming HSTU and Wukong. They say scaling several dimensions together is needed for consistent gains. They say model and input scale, plus features, drove performance more than architecture changes, which mainly mattered for training stability.
record.recipe_differences: This is a LinkedIn recommender-ranking study, not a language-model pretraining scaling-law experiment; it reports ranking evaluation loss and AUC rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy, and does not fit power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by which dimension is scaled in isolation: sequence length shows clear scaling across metrics, while layer count and ID embedding dimension do not consistently scale evaluation loss and show irregular or plateauing Contributions AUC.

fits_no_version.finding: Ranking AUC (Long Dwell, Contributions) rises with training FLOPS: Long Dwell gains ~0.015 per order of magnitude. In isolated layer and embedding-dim sweeps, Long Dwell AUC rises while Contributions AUC is irregular or plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task metrics of recommender ranking models improve log-linearly with training compute when model dimensions are scaled jointly.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing LiGR layers with HSTU layers gives a lower scaling curve. At 1e17 FLOPS, Long Dwell AUC is 75.87 vs 76.03. Doubling the ID vocabulary (33M to 66M) gave no AUC difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recommender scaling curves depend on layer architecture, and sparse-embedding parameter growth need not improve performance.

record.problems: The results concern recommender ranking rather than language-model pretraining. The paper does not report fitted exponents, an optimal compute allocation, or numerical values for most plotted curves; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-law result rows left out. Other experiments, including feature ablations, retrieval measurements, setwise-ranking comparisons and A/B tests, do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count on loss. The appendix gives only anecdotal AUC remarks.
No power-law fit or exponent, so the power-law form in ranking is not established. Image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning regimes are not tested.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or data choices.

missing.what: LiGR vs HSTU scaling curves on normalized entropy and AUC, including Long Dwell AUC 76.03 vs 75.87 at 1e17 FLOPS
missing.locator: §5.1 'Scaling law of LiGR vs HSTU'; Figures 6-9
missing.versions: none (architecture-dependence of scaling curve in ranking)

missing.what: No AUC difference between 33M and 66M ID-embedding vocabularies

record.verdict_notes: No power-law fits or exponents anywhere; 'scaling law' is used loosely for monotone trends against log FLOPS. Compute excludes the sparse embedding parameters. Training was on 8 A100s with about 4M evaluation samples; no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study is about recommender ranking, not held-out language-model pretraining loss.
It does not fit power laws on small language-model runs or test predictions on larger runs.
It does not identify a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.
It does not compare depth and width at a fixed parameter count for language-model pretraining loss.

Tests scaling in recommender ranking, but not other modalities such as image or video generation, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer; it does not fit and report a power-law form or exponents.
It reports ranking-task metrics, not downstream language-model task performance or its relationship to language-model pretraining loss.

Tests whether scaling outcomes vary when individual model dimensions are changed, but does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules or data choices; it does not estimate exponents or a compute-optimal split.

relationships.condition: LiGR feed ranking, joint scaling of dense params, sequence length and embedding dim; and sequence-length-only scaling
relationships.reason: Evaluation loss falls steadily with log training FLOPS and with sequence length (R1, R4). These rest on figures only, with no fitted power law.
relationships.display_finding: Evaluation loss decreased steadily with log training FLOPs and sequence length, without a fitted power law.

relationships.condition: Scaling transformer layers alone or ID-embedding dimension alone, other dims fixed
relationships.reason: Text says these do not consistently scale evaluation loss, so loss gains need joint scaling (R7, R10). This resembles the bottleneck caveat.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing transformer layers or ID-embedding dimension alone did not consistently improve evaluation loss, indicating a need for joint scaling.
